section.title: I Will Extol You, My God and King
section.sectionRationale: The last psalm attributed to David and the only one titled a psalm of praise, this alphabetic acrostic, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, gathers every theme of the Psalter, God's greatness, compassion, kingdom, and nearness, into a single sustained hymn that opens the five unbroken Hallelujah psalms closing the whole book, 146-150.
section.thesis: David extols the LORD as his God and King from A to Z of the Hebrew alphabet, declaring that His greatness is unsearchable, His compassion rests on all He has made, His kingdom is everlasting, and He is near to all who call on Him in truth, an all-encompassing praise that invites every generation, and every living thing, to bless His holy name forever.
section.frameNote: Six movements following the acrostic's flow: unending personal praise, verses 1-3; generation to generation declaring His mighty acts, verses 4-7; His gracious and compassionate character, verses 8-9; His everlasting kingdom, verses 10-13; His provision for every living thing, verses 14-16; and His nearness, justice, and the closing call for all creation to bless His name, verses 17-21.

units.label: I will exalt You, my God and King

verses.text: I will exalt You, my God and King; I will bless Your name forever and ever.
Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever.
Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised; His greatness is {{cheker|unsearchable}}.

units.label: One generation will commend Your works
units.note: generational declaration of God's mighty acts

verses.text: One generation will commend Your works to the next, and will proclaim Your mighty acts,
the glorious splendor of Your majesty. And I will meditate on Your wondrous works.
They will proclaim the power of Your awesome deeds, and I will declare Your greatness.
They will extol the fame of Your abundant goodness and sing joyfully of Your righteousness.

units.label: The LORD is gracious and compassionate

verses.text: The LORD is {{channun|gracious}} and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion.
The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made.

units.label: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom

verses.text: All You have made will give You thanks, O LORD, and Your saints will bless You.
They will tell of the glory of Your kingdom and speak of Your might,
to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom.
Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations. The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions.
The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down.
The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season.
You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing.

units.label: The LORD is near to all who call on Him
units.note: nearness, justice, and the call to bless His name

verses.text: The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds.
The LORD is {{qarov|near}} to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth.
He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them.
The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy.
My mouth will declare the praise of the LORD; let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever.

cheker.gloss: Searching out, an investigable limit. God's greatness is described as ein cheker, without limit or searching out, meaning it exceeds every human attempt to fully comprehend or measure it.

channun.gloss: Gracious, showing unearned favor. Paired here with compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in loving devotion, this is the classic fourfold description of God's character first revealed to Moses, Exodus 34:6.

qarov.gloss: Near, close at hand. The LORD's nearness is not automatic but is promised specifically to all who call on Him in truth, verse 18, showing that access to God's presence is real, personal, and available to anyone who seeks Him sincerely.

basic.context: David's final psalm is an alphabetic acrostic, each verse beginning with the next successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a comprehensive, A to Z hymn of praise gathering God's greatness, compassion, everlasting kingdom, and provision for all creation into a single sustained song.
basic.hermeneutics: The acrostic form itself teaches completeness, praise that runs the full alphabet, leaving nothing about God's character unsung. The psalm describes David's own resolve to praise every day forever; it prescribes the same all-encompassing, daily praise as the fitting response to who God has revealed Himself to be.
basic.originalLanguages: God's greatness has no cheker, no searching out or limit, verse 3. He is channun, gracious, paired with compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in loving devotion, the classic fourfold description first revealed to Moses, Exodus 34:6. And He is qarov, near, to all who call on Him in truth, verse 18, real access promised to any sincere seeker.
basic.typology: The psalm's vision of an everlasting kingdom, verse 13, anticipates Jesus' own announcement, the kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matthew 4:17, while its picture of God opening His hand to satisfy every living thing, verse 16, anticipates Christ's miracles of feeding multitudes, Mark 6:30-44, and God's final, perfect provision in the new creation.
basic.christ: This psalm's confession that the LORD is near to all who call on Him in truth, verse 18, is fulfilled and deepened in Christ, through whom believers now have access to the Father, Ephesians 2:18, and its vision of an everlasting kingdom is realized in Jesus, the Son of David whose throne and kingdom will never end, Luke 1:32-33.
basic.god: God is exalted as unsearchably great yet personally near, gracious and compassionate to all He has made, faithful to every word and kind in every deed, the King whose everlasting kingdom sustains, provides for, and hears the cry of everyone who calls on Him in truth.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 34:6 is the source of the fourfold description echoed in verse 8, gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. Matthew 6:26 develops the psalm's picture of God's provision for every living thing. Romans 10:13 echoes verse 18's promise that all who call on Him will be heard.
basic.oneStory: David's alphabet of praise, gathering God's unsearchable greatness, His grace to all He has made, His everlasting kingdom, and His nearness to every sincere caller, finds its fulfillment in Christ, in whom believers have access to the Father and through whom God's kingdom, promised here to endure forever, is finally and fully established.

context.literary:
The acrostic does more than organise the praise; it shapes how the praise is heard. The first and last verses carry the same refrain, 'bless Your name forever and ever,' verses 1, 2 and 21, and the first verse begins with 'I' and the last with 'my mouth.' The song is an envelope: a single voice opens and closes it, and the whole of creation is gathered in between. The heading, which the Hebrew calls a tehillah, a praise, is the only one of its kind in the Psalter, and the final verse ends with the same word, so the book that bears the name Praises has its name at the heart of this psalm.

Inside the frame the voices keep changing. In verses 4 to 7 'I' and 'they' alternate: one generation will commend, 'I will meditate,' they will proclaim, 'I will declare,' they will extol. The singer does not stand alone but threads his own voice through a chorus from every generation. In verses 10 to 12 the 'works' sing back to their maker, and the saints tell the kingdom to men. Then the psalm turns from praise about God to praise to God and back, as the person shifts between 'You' and 'He.'

The word 'all' carries the poem: every day, to all, all He has made, all generations, all who fall, the eyes of all, every living thing, all who call, all who love Him. A reader who counts the instances feels the psalm refusing to leave anyone out. The kingdom verse falls at the centre of the alphabet, and it is followed by the verses on care, upholding, feeding, nearness, so that the royal title is immediately given a face: this King lifts up the bowed.

The missing nun line, supplied in the BSB at the end of verse 13, ends with 'kind in all His actions,' and verse 17 closes with almost the same words, 'kind in all His deeds.' The psalm says its most important thing twice.
context.historical:
The acrostic was a recognised form in Israel. Psalms 9 and 10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112 and 119, Proverbs 31:10-31 and the first four chapters of Lamentations all use the alphabet as a frame. It served memory and completeness, and for a teaching psalm meant to be passed from parent to child, as verse 4 insists, the alphabet was a practical aid. Psalm 145 uses it for praise rather than lament or instruction, and it uses it on the largest scale.

The speaker is a king who calls God 'my God and King.' In the ancient Near East, the great king was the figure of power, and the title is a quiet reorientation. David holds the throne of Israel because a greater King has given it to him. The language of verses 3 to 13 is close to David's blessing at the gathering of the people before Solomon's reign, where he says that the greatness, the power, the glory, the splendor and the majesty belong to the LORD, and that His is the kingdom, 1 Chronicles 29:10-13. The royal prayer and the royal psalm draw on the same vocabulary of kingship.

The covenant behind it is the one made with David, in which his house and kingdom were promised to endure, 2 Samuel 7:16. The psalm lifts the eye from the house of David to the kingdom of God that stands behind it, 'an everlasting kingdom,' verse 13. Nebuchadnezzar, after his humbling, uses almost the same words in Daniel 4:34, so the confession reaches pagan kings too.

The psalm has had a long life in worship. Jewish tradition has prized it, and the Talmud commends reciting it three times a day, partly because it is an alphabet of praise and partly because of the line about the open hand. It stands at the heart of the daily prayer known as Ashrei. Christians have long used verses 15 and 16 as a table grace. The psalm is a song for ordinary days, for work and meals and the passing on of faith to children.
context.canonical:
Psalm 145 is the last psalm in the Psalter headed with David's name, and it is placed at the hinge of the book. Behind it are five Davidic laments and prayers, Psalms 140 to 144, and after it come five psalms that begin and end with Hallelujah, Psalms 146 to 150. Many of the themes of verse 14 return in Psalm 146:8, 'the LORD lifts those who are weighed down,' and the last line of the Psalter, 'Let everything that has breath praise the LORD,' Psalm 150:6, echoes the 'every creature' of verse 21.

Verse 8 draws on the oldest creed of Israel. After the golden calf, the LORD revealed Himself to Moses as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' Exodus 34:6. The formula is repeated through the Old Testament: Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Nehemiah 9:17, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2. Each time it is used in a new situation: in worship, in confession, in a prophet's call to repentance, and in Jonah's angry complaint that God was merciful to Nineveh. Psalm 145 takes it as a ground for universal praise.

The picture of God's open hand draws on Psalm 104:27-28, 'You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good things,' and Psalm 36:6, 'You preserve man and beast.' Isaiah speaks of the God whose understanding is 'beyond searching out,' Isaiah 40:28, with the same word that the psalm uses of His greatness. The kingdom language joins Exodus 15:18, Daniel 4:3 and Daniel 7:14.

The New Testament takes the psalm into the prayer of Jesus. 'Your kingdom come' and 'Give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:10-11, are verses 13 and 15 to 16 in the mouth of the Son. Jesus teaches that the Father feeds the birds, Matthew 6:26, and Paul tells the Athenians and the people of Lystra that God did not leave Himself without a witness, giving rain and fruitful seasons, Acts 14:17. Revelation 15:3-4 sings of the King of the nations whose works are great and whose ways are just, and Revelation 5:13 has every creature saying praise to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm's first aim is to make praise a habit that outlasts the singer. 'Every day' and 'forever and ever' stand next to 'one generation to the next,' so the author is not content with a private devotion. He wants a people to be formed who tell their children what God has done, so that the knowledge of God is never one generation old.

His second aim is to widen the hearers' sense of who God is. The psalm moves from the king who prays, to the saints who speak, to all He has made, to every living thing that looks to Him for food. A people who thought God belonged to them alone were being shown that His compassion rests on 'all He has made,' and that their own song was only the lead voice in a choir that includes every creature.

Third, he wants the hearers to trust God's nearness. The God whose greatness cannot be searched out is also close to everyone who calls on Him in truth. The two truths are meant to be held together, so that awe does not turn into distance and nearness does not turn into familiarity.

Finally, he wants his people to live with moral seriousness. The psalm closes with the destruction of the wicked, and it does so after saying that God is righteous in all His ways. The author did not want praise to be an escape from the world's injustice but a way of seeing that the God who is good to all will in the end set things right.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes who God is and what David resolved to do. Its statements about God are meant as truths to be believed by every reader: He is gracious, He is great, He is near, and His kingdom lasts. Its vows, 'I will exalt,' 'every day I will bless,' are David's own, yet they are offered as a pattern, and the psalm expects the same response from every generation and every creature.

Some of its sweeping statements need care in application. 'You give them their food in season' and 'satisfy the desire of every living thing' describe God's general provision. They do not promise that no believer will ever go hungry, since Scripture records famine and persecution among the faithful, Hebrews 11:37. Likewise, 'He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him' is bounded by fearing Him, and it is to be read with the New Testament's reminder that He hears us when we ask according to His will, 1 John 5:14. It is not a blank cheque.

The last line about the destruction of the wicked is a statement about God's action at the end, not a licence for His people to do it. What is clearly for us is the practice of daily praise, telling the next generation, and calling on Him in truth.

debates.question: Why is the nun line missing from the traditional Hebrew text, and does it matter?

views.label: It was lost in copying and later restored
views.case: The BSB footnote says the final two lines of verse 13 are supplied by one Hebrew manuscript, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Dead Sea Scrolls. The line fits the acrostic exactly, and its wording closely matches the second half of verse 17, which makes it look original rather than invented.

views.label: The acrostic was never strictly complete
views.case: Not every biblical acrostic follows the alphabet without a flaw, and a deliberate or very early gap cannot be fully excluded. On this view the gap is a feature of the text as received, and the line in other versions is a later repair.

views.label: The gap was noticed and theologically explained in tradition
views.case: Jewish tradition explained the missing letter in various ways. These explanations are interpretations, not evidence of the original shape, but they show how seriously the community treated the full alphabet.

debates.bearing: The balance of evidence favours restoring the line. In either case the psalm's teaching is not harmed, since the same truth, that God is faithful and kind, stands in verse 17 as well.

debates.question: How can God be 'good to all' in verse 9 and yet destroy 'all the wicked' in verse 20?

views.label: Common goodness now, final judgment later
views.case: Matthew 5:45 says God sends sun and rain on the evil and the good. His present kindness is real and wide, and Romans 2:4 says it is meant to lead to repentance. Judgment is the end of those who finally refuse Him, as 2 Peter 3:9 and Acts 17:31 teach.

views.label: The 'wicked' are those who persist in rejecting Him
views.case: The psalm separates people by their response: those who call on Him in truth, who fear Him, who love Him, and the wicked who do not. Nineveh, in Jonah 4:2 and 4:10-11, shows God's mercy offered even to the wicked when they turn.

views.label: Goodness to creation is distinct from salvation of every person
views.case: The 'all' of verses 9 and 15 to 16 is plainly about creatures and provision. Verse 19 and verse 20 are about the saving relationship, and the psalm does not claim that every person will be saved.

debates.bearing: The psalm holds mercy and justice side by side without apology. God's goodness is not weakened by the judgment, and the judgment is not cruelty, because it falls on those who refuse the One who is near to all who call.

debates.question: Is the 'everlasting kingdom' of verse 13 a present reality or a future hope?

views.label: A present reality
views.case: The verbs of verses 13 to 20 are in the present: He upholds, lifts up, opens His hand, is near. The kingdom is God's rule over all that He has made now, as in Psalm 10:16 and Exodus 15:18.

views.label: A future hope still to be seen
views.case: Much of the psalm uses future verbs, 'will tell,' 'will give thanks,' and the New Testament looks for the day when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, Revelation 11:15.

views.label: Both, in the pattern of 'already and not yet'
views.case: Jesus announces that the kingdom is near, Mark 1:15, and yet teaches His people to pray 'Your kingdom come,' Matthew 6:10. God's rule is real now and is not yet fully acknowledged.

debates.bearing: The third view fits best the way the psalm and the New Testament speak. God reigns now, and His reign will be seen by all, and the believer lives and praises in the space between.

study.originalLanguages:
The vocabulary of Psalm 145 is carefully chosen. The word 'works,' ma'aseh, is a thread through the poem. It appears for the works to be commended in verse 4, for 'all He has made' in verse 9, for 'all You have made' in verse 10, and in 'kind in all His actions' in verses 13 and 17. The works of God, His creation and His deeds, are what the psalm asks everyone to praise, and the same word ties the world to the one who made it.

In verse 7 the verb translated 'extol' is a word of overflow: it is the verb of Psalm 19:2, 'Day after day they pour forth speech.' The fame of God's goodness gushes out, and the singer cannot keep it in. Verse 9 says that His compassion rests on all He has made. The word for compassion is built on the word for the womb, so God's mercy is the tender feeling of a parent for what it has borne.

The word 'kind' in verses 13 and 17 is chasid, and in verse 10 the same root names God's 'saints,' chasidim. God is chasid in all His deeds, and His people are His chasidim, so that the faithful are meant to reflect their Maker's loyal love. 'Righteous in all His ways' in verse 17 and 'kind in all His deeds' belong together: His justice and His mercy are never at odds.

In verse 14 the verb 'upholds' is somech, to support or prop, used in Psalm 3:5, 'the LORD sustains me,' and Psalm 37:24, 'the LORD is holding his hand.' Verse 15 says the eyes of all 'look' to Him, using a verb of hopeful waiting, the same one in Psalm 104:27. The 'open hand' of verse 16 is the same picture as that psalm, and Psalm 146:8 repeats the phrase 'lifts those who are weighed down.'

The 'desire' of verses 16 and 19 is ratson, a word that can also mean favour or good pleasure, as in Psalm 30:5, 'His favor lasts a lifetime,' and in Psalm 143:10, where it is translated 'will.' God satisfies what He Himself delights to give. Finally, 'every creature' in verse 21 is literally 'all flesh,' the same breadth as the 'every living thing' of verse 16, and the Psalter's closing line widens it to 'everything that has breath,' Psalm 150:6.

typology.type: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The psalm speaks of a kingdom that outlasts all generations. Daniel sees one like a son of man given 'an everlasting dominion that will not pass away,' Daniel 7:14, and Gabriel promises Mary that her Son will receive David's throne and that 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32-33. The correspondence is the kingdom without end; the escalation is that it now has a King who is both David's son and God's. It falls short of the whole story in being general. The psalm does not yet say that the King will die and rise to make it so.

typology.type: You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing, verses 15 and 16
typology.fulfillment: God's open hand becomes a human hand in the feeding of the crowds. Jesus gives thanks, breaks and gives, and 'they all ate and were satisfied,' Mark 6:41-42; John 6:11 adds 'as much as they wanted.' Then He says 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, which moves the gift from the table to the giver. The type falls short because the loaves feed a crowd for a day. The Lamb will lead His people to springs of living water, so that they never hunger or thirst again, Revelation 7:16-17.

typology.type: The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: In a synagogue Jesus sees a woman who had been bent double for eighteen years, calls her over, tells her she is free, and 'immediately she straightened up,' Luke 13:10-13. The verb of lifting in the psalm becomes a hand laid on a bent back. The type falls short because the woman would bend again with age and die. The promise of the psalm reaches its end when Christ raises His people from the dead, and no one is left bowed down.

typology.type: The LORD is near to all who call on Him, verse 18
typology.fulfillment: Moses marvelled that no other god is so near to a nation as the LORD is whenever Israel calls, Deuteronomy 4:7. In Jesus, nearness takes a human face. He is Immanuel, God with us, and the apostles proclaimed that the kingdom was near, Mark 1:15. Believers who were far away are 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13, and may approach the throne with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. The nearness is now through the Spirit and by faith; the full nearness is in the new creation, where they will see His face, Revelation 22:4.

study.christ:
Psalm 145 does not name the Messiah, but it is a psalm of David about the King of all kings, and every one of its large claims is taken up in the New Testament as true of Jesus. Start with the kingdom. The psalm calls God's rule an everlasting kingdom and a dominion for all generations, and the angel tells Mary that her Son will take David's throne, that He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and that 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32-33. When Jesus begins to preach, His message is 'the kingdom of God is near,' Mark 1:15. Revelation says that 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 11:15. The psalm's King and David's Son are one.

The creed of verse 8 has its human face in Him. John says the Word became flesh and was 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, the New Testament's rendering of the loving devotion and faithfulness of Exodus 34:6, and adds that no one has seen God, but the Son 'has made Him known,' John 1:17-18. The psalm's catalogue of God's character is what Jesus shows in His healing of the bent, His patience with the slow, His welcome of the outcast.

The open hand becomes the hand that breaks the loaves, Mark 6:41-42, and the One who feeds also teaches us to ask, 'Give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:11, in the same prayer that says 'Your kingdom come.' Nearness takes its fullest form in Him. Paul quotes Joel's promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved and applies it to Jesus as Lord of all, who gives richly to all who call, Romans 10:12-13, and Ephesians 2:13-18 says that those who were far away have been brought near and now have access to the Father.

The last verse of the psalm looks forward to the day when 'every creature' blesses the holy name, and Revelation 5:13 shows it: every creature in heaven and on earth and in the sea says, 'To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever.' The Lamb is included in the song to God.

There is a sober side too. The One who is near to all who call is also the Judge appointed by God, Acts 17:31, and the psalm's last verses about the wicked are not set aside. A fair reading holds both: the Lord is the friend of those who call on Him, and the final word on those who will not.
study.god:
Psalm 145 gives one of the fullest portraits of God in the Old Testament, and it takes care to balance its parts. First it shows His transcendence. His greatness is 'unsearchable,' a word Isaiah applies to His understanding, Isaiah 40:28, and Job asks whether anyone can fathom the deep things of God, Job 11:7. The psalm does not hide the fact that we cannot map Him. Yet in the same verses where His majesty is beyond limit, He is also 'near to all who call on Him,' verse 18. The doctrine of God that follows is of One who is both incomprehensible and approachable, and the two truths come together in worship, where we are allowed to speak to the One we cannot exhaust.

It shows His character through the creed. He is gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, verse 8. Slowness to anger is not weakness; Nahum 1:3 says He is slow to anger and great in power, and will not leave the guilty unpunished. The psalm keeps both sides, the creed in verse 8 and the judgment of the wicked in verse 20. God's kindness is not a mood. It is the consistent shape of His action: 'righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds,' verse 17.

It shows His generosity as the pattern of His rule. He is a king who feeds His subjects, and the order matters: provision comes before demand. His hand is open, and it is open to every living thing. The Creator has made a world in which, by His design, each creature has food in season, and the psalm reads that ordinary pattern as a sign of the heart of God. A theology that began with His sovereignty alone would miss this; sovereignty in this psalm is expressed as care.

It shows His particular attention. The circles tighten as the psalm proceeds: He is good to all, He lifts those who fall, He is near to those who call, He fulfils the desires of those who fear Him, He preserves those who love Him. Wide mercy and personal closeness are not rivals. He is the God of the whole world and He knows each one who cries.

For worship, the psalm teaches completeness and constancy. Praise should run from the first letter to the last and from the first day to the last, and it should include the telling of His works to the next generation. We bless a King who is worthy of every word, and who loves to be called on.

crossReferences.note: The revelation to Moses after the golden calf, from which verse 8 draws its four phrases. The psalm leaves out the closing lines about forgiveness and judgment here, but returns to judgment in verse 20, so the whole creed is held.
Jonah quotes the same creed as the reason he did not want to preach to Nineveh. It shows the creed's edge: the God who is 'good to all' really does mean all, and a prophet can be offended by it.

'His understanding is beyond searching out.' The same word as the 'unsearchable' of verse 3, applied to God's mind. It confirms that the greatness praised here is not only power but wisdom beyond measure.

'Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?' The question to which verse 3 replies. It shows that the limits of our understanding are an old theme, and that the right response is praise.

David's blessing before the assembly, with greatness, power, glory, splendor, majesty and kingdom all ascribed to the LORD. It shows that the royal vocabulary of Psalm 145 came from the king's own prayer.

Nebuchadnezzar says that God's dominion is an everlasting dominion and His kingdom endures from generation to generation, nearly verse 13. It shows that this confession can reach a pagan emperor who has been humbled.

'All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season... You open Your hand.' The nearest parallel to verses 15 and 16, with the same verb of hopeful looking. It shows how the Psalter linked creation with continued provision.

'Your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?' Jesus draws a conclusion from the same open hand, and applies it to anxiety. It shows how the psalm's general provision becomes a personal assurance.
'The LORD lifts those who are weighed down.' The same words as verse 14, opening the Hallelujah psalms. It shows that the praise of Psalm 145 flows straight into the final five psalms.
Israel's wonder that no other nation has a god so near whenever they call. It is the background to verse 18 and makes plain that the nearness is not a mood but a feature of the covenant.
Paul says the same Lord is Lord of all and gives richly to all who call, quoting Joel 2:32. It shows that verse 18's call is, in the New Testament, a call on the name of Jesus.

Every creature in heaven and on earth and in the sea praises Him who sits on the throne and the Lamb. It is the fullest answer to the last verse of the psalm, 'let every creature bless His holy name.'

study.oneStory:
The psalm begins before the fall. In the first chapter of the Bible God gives food to every creature, 'everything that has the breath of life in it,' Genesis 1:29-30, and the open hand of verse 16 is that first gift continued. 'All He has made' recalls the 'very good' of creation, and the psalm's refusal to leave any creature out is a refusal to forget what was made.

The fall did not cancel this goodness. After the flood God promises that seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth endures, Genesis 8:21-22, and He makes a covenant with 'every living creature,' Genesis 9:9-10. The food that arrives in its season, even from a cursed ground, is a sign of that promise. So when David says that God's compassion rests on all He has made, he is standing on the covenant with Noah as much as on the covenant with Israel.

The creed of verse 8 belongs to the story of redemption, since God spoke it to Moses after Israel had worshipped a calf and still would not abandon them, Exodus 34:6. The kingdom of verse 13 is the line that runs from the exodus, 'The LORD will reign forever and ever,' Exodus 15:18, to David's throne, 2 Samuel 7:16, to the Son of David, Luke 1:32-33. The commission to tell the next generation, verse 4, becomes the commission to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19-20, with the Lord's promise to be with His people always.

The psalm's final verse is the shape of the last chapter. Paul says creation itself waits to be set free from decay, Romans 8:19-21, and John hears every creature praising Him who sits on the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 5:13. In the new creation the thirsty are satisfied, Revelation 7:16-17, the dwelling of God is with man, and no one has to call out to a distant God. The alphabet of praise reaches its last letter, and the song goes on 'forever and ever.'

sermon.title: One Generation Shall Praise Your Works to Another
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly from Psalm 145:4, showing that it is the biblical duty of every generation to make sure the next generation hears about God's mighty acts, with exultation rather than mere information, applying this psalm's generational vision pastorally to parents and churches.

quiz.q: What literary form structures this entire psalm?

options.text: An alphabetic acrostic, with each verse beginning with the next successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
options.note: This acrostic structure, noted in the BSB's own footnote, pictures comprehensive, A to Z praise of God.

options.text: A strict historical narrative recounting the reigns of Israel's kings.
options.note: The psalm is a hymn of praise structured as an acrostic, not a historical narrative of kings' reigns.

options.text: A legal contract between David and the LORD.
options.note: The psalm is worship and praise, not a legal document or contract.

options.text: A riddle intended to be solved by the reader.
options.note: The acrostic form organizes praise systematically; it is not designed as a riddle to solve.

quiz.q: How does David describe God's greatness in verse 3?

options.text: As unsearchable, beyond any human ability to fully measure or comprehend.
options.note: The Hebrew phrase behind unsearchable indicates greatness with no limit that can be searched out.

options.text: As easily measured and fully understood by human wisdom.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that God's greatness is unsearchable, exceeding human comprehension.

options.text: As limited to only a few specific attributes.
options.note: The verse describes greatness without any stated limit, not a narrow set of traits.

options.text: As diminishing with the passing of each generation.
options.note: The following verses show each generation proclaiming God's greatness anew, not describing it as fading.

quiz.q: What fourfold description of God's character appears in verse 8?

options.text: Gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion.
options.note: This classic description echoes God's own self-revelation to Moses in Exodus 34:6.

options.text: Distant, harsh, quick to anger, and sparing in mercy.
options.note: The verse describes the opposite qualities, nearness, grace, patience, and abundant mercy.

options.text: Wealthy, powerful, feared, and unapproachable.
options.note: The description focuses on relational, merciful qualities, not wealth or unapproachable power.

options.text: Silent, indifferent, unpredictable, and cold.
options.note: The verse describes a warm, gracious, patient, and loving character, not silence or indifference.

quiz.q: According to verse 18, to whom is the LORD near?

options.text: To all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth.
options.note: This promise of nearness is tied specifically to sincere, truthful calling on God's name.

options.text: Only to kings and rulers, never to ordinary people.
options.note: The verse says all who call on Him, without restriction to social or political status.

options.text: To no one, since God remains entirely distant from creation.
options.note: The verse explicitly affirms God's nearness, the opposite of total distance.

options.text: Only to those born into the nation of Israel.
options.note: The promise is extended to all who call on Him in truth, not restricted by ethnicity or birth.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's final verse call all creation to respond?

options.text: By joining David's mouth in declaring the LORD's praise, with every creature blessing His holy name forever and ever.
options.note: Verse 21 extends the call to praise beyond David personally to every creature, forever.

options.text: By remaining silent out of reverent fear.
options.note: The verse calls for vocal declaration and blessing of God's name, not silence.

options.text: By limiting praise only to the priests in the temple.
options.note: The call is universal, every creature, not restricted to a priestly class.

options.text: By ending all praise once David himself had died.
options.note: The call is for praise forever and ever, extending well beyond David's own lifetime.

questions: This psalm systematically praises God from A to Z, leaving nothing about His character unsung. What aspect of God's character have you neglected to praise Him for recently?
David commits to bless God every day, forever. What would it look like to build a daily rhythm of praise into your life this week, rather than praising God only in crisis or celebration?

The psalm calls one generation to commend God's works to the next. Who is the next generation in your life, children, younger believers, newer Christians, and what mighty acts of God could you be telling them about?
God's compassion rests on all He has made, and He is near to all who call on Him in truth. Is there an area of your life where you have been calling on God only halfheartedly rather than in truth?
The psalm's final call is for every creature to bless God's holy name forever. How does joining that ongoing, eternal chorus of praise change the way you see your own worship today?

translationNotes.note: The BSB notes that this psalm is an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet, a feature that shapes the psalm's comprehensive, all-encompassing scope of praise.

The BSB notes that its final two lines, the LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions, are supplied from one Masoretic Text manuscript, the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Dead Sea Scrolls, restoring the traditional verse for the Hebrew letter nun, missing in most Masoretic manuscripts.
Every creature renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning all flesh, extending the call to bless God's name to the whole created order, not merely to Israel or to humanity alone.
